passages.english: "But one who is free of sin is free also of this kind of conception." Did holy Ambrose, by the truth of this statement of his, condemn the goodness of marriage, and not rather the emptiness of these heretics, although they had not yet appeared at that time? I thought this worth mentioning because Pelagius praises Ambrose so highly as to say: "The blessed bishop Ambrose, in whose books above all the Roman faith shines out, who blossomed as a kind of beautiful flower among Latin writers, whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures not even an enemy has dared to criticise" (Book
passages.notes: The citation breaks off at the end of the passage; the context shows it continues "3 [or similar] On Free Will" (Pelagius, Pro libero arbitrio). Numerous scanning errors corrected (e.g. 'exp rs' = expers, 'ha rcticorum' = haereticorum, 'erriluit' = effloruit, 'r.c' = ne).

passages.english: Or if you boast that even that most faithful man held this view in the manner of the Manichaeans, boast it, boast it, so that you may fill up the measure of Jovinian more completely: together with that man of God we patiently endure your curses and insults. And yet your heresiarch Pelagius so praises the faith and the most pure understanding of the Scriptures of Ambrose that he says not even an enemy dared to find fault with it. Consider, then, how far you have gone, and restrain yourselves at long last from the daring of Jovinian. Although he, by praising marriage too much, made it equal to holy virginity;
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (pcrfectius, cnm, ha;resiarches, ct, Soripturis). The footnote mark '1' after 'perfectius' omitted. 'Ausibus' is taken as 'acts of daring' (from ausum). The sentence continues into the following passage.

passages.original: ID uno IUliine jure vituperatur intentio, et natura laudatur, quia duo suat quæ contrariis applicentur : sed eliam in parvulo, non unum est lanium, id est, natura, in qnia crcaius csl homo a Deo hono; habet enim et vitium, quod per unum in omnes homines pertransiit, sicut sapit Apostolus, non sicut desipit Pelagius, vel Cœlestius, vel corum quicumque discipulus. Horum * itaque duorum, quæ in parvulo esse diximus, unum adscribitur Deo, alterum diabolo. Et quod utrumque propter unum horum, id est, propter vitium, subjicitur potestati diaboli, ideo non est incongruum, quia non fit ipsius diaboli potestate, sed Dei.
passages.english: In a single person it is right that the intention is blamed and the nature praised, because they are two things to which contrary [judgements] are applied. But in an infant too there is not one thing only, that is, the nature in which man was created by the good God; for it also has the fault which passed through one man into all men, as the Apostle wisely says, not as Pelagius, or Caelestius, or any disciple of theirs foolishly says. Of these two things, then, which we have said are in an infant, one is ascribed to God, the other to the devil. And that both, on account of one of them, that is, on account of the fault, are made subject to the power of the devil is therefore not inappropriate, because this does not come about by the power of the devil himself, but by that of God.
passages.notes: The opening 'ID uno IUliine jure' is badly garbled; read as 'In uno homine jure'. Other scanning errors corrected (e.g. 'lanium' = tantum, 'sapit/desipit' play on wise/foolish).

passages.english: so that the Pelagians, whichever of them by a vow of continence do not enjoy carnal marriage, may delight in it, if not by its use, at least by its praises. Only let him spare infants, so that he does not praise them uselessly and defend them cruelly; let him not say that they are saved, [but] let him allow them to come not to Pelagius their praiser, but to Christ their Saviour. For let this book now be closed here, since his discourse, which is written in the paper you sent, ended in such a way that he said: "Truly believe that all things were made through Jesus, and without him nothing was made";
passages.notes: 'tantum parvulis parcat' may be read with the preceding as referring to Julian (the 'iste' of the context). 'salvos esse non dicat' read as 'let him not [merely] call them saved'; the sense is that he should not declare them already safe without Christ. Scanning errors corrected (e.g. 'chatula' = chartula, 'sirne ipso factum tal mihil' = sine ipso factum est nihil).
